Camera animation and interaction

Source: vignettes/motion.Rmd
motion.Rmd

Camera motion shows a fixed scene from several directions. Data animation changes the observations or geometry between states. This article renders both kinds of animation and opens a panel with orbit controls. Installation is covered in Get started. Movie output uses gifski for GIF files or av for MP4 files; the viewer uses htmlwidgets.

  1. Build the scene with coord_3d().

  2. Render a camera path with animate_3d().

  3. Explore the plot with view_3d().

Example 

library(ggplot2)
library(ggplot3d)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 17) + theme(
  plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.key = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.box.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.position = "none"))
d <- expand.grid(x = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 12),
                 y = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 12))
d$z <- with(d, exp(-(x^2 + y^2) / 2))
p <- ggplot(d, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_surface_3d(fill = "#2E6F9E") +
  coord_3d(azimuth = -60, elevation = 30, frame = "azimuth")

The data describe a curved surface sampled on a regular grid. The camera looks toward the centre of its expanded box.

p

Save a camera path

The default path makes a full azimuth turn. Each frame retains the panel dimensions and framing bounds; the final angle precedes the starting angle so a loop repeats each view once. The result records the rendering time of each frame in seconds.

if (requireNamespace("gifski", quietly = TRUE)) {
  path <- tempfile(fileext = ".gif")
  movie <- animate_3d(p, frames = 12, fps = 6, file = path,
                     width = 480, height = 480, progress = FALSE)
  data.frame(frames = movie$frame_count, fps = movie$fps,
             file_written = file.exists(movie$file))
  range(movie$timings)
  unlink(path)
}

Camera arguments accept a scalar, a vector with one value per frame, or a function of time in seconds. This path raises the camera while it rotates. Varying elevation or roll uses sphere framing, which reserves bounds for arbitrary rotation.

frames <- animate_3d(p, frames = 3, fps = 2,
  azimuth = function(t) -60 + 90 * t,
  elevation = c(20, 35, 50), renderer = "vector",
  width = 320, height = 320, progress = FALSE)
frames$camera
#>   time azimuth elevation zoom roll   projection fov distance target_x target_y
#> 1  0.0     -60        20    1    0 orthographic  35       NA      0.5      0.5
#> 2  0.5     -15        35    1    0 orthographic  35       NA      0.5      0.5
#> 3  1.0      30        50    1    0 orthographic  35       NA      0.5      0.5
#>   target_z
#> 1      0.5
#> 2      0.5
#> 3      0.5
frames$panel_extents[[1]]
#> $`panel.9-7-9-7.scene-panel-3d`
#>  width_mm height_mm 
#>  37.08663  37.08663
unlink(dirname(frames$frames[1]), recursive = TRUE)

Raster rendering is the default. Selecting vector rendering uses the exact vector scene backend to produce each PNG frame, and an output filename ending in .mp4 selects the video encoder.

if (requireNamespace("av", quietly = TRUE)) {
  path <- tempfile(fileext = ".mp4")
  movie <- animate_3d(p, frames = 3, fps = 6, file = path,
                     width = 320, height = 320, progress = FALSE)
  file.exists(movie$file)
  unlink(path)
}

Tween observations between states

The time argument selects a column naming the states. Layers without that column appear in every frame. The following example uses three cars from the built-in data, then constructs a hypothetical second state with lower weight and two more miles per gallon. Each car keeps its model name as its group, including when the second state’s rows are reversed.

observed <- mtcars[c(1, 3, 8), c("wt", "hp", "mpg")]
observed$id <- rownames(observed)
observed$state <- 0
changed <- transform(observed[3:1, ], wt = wt * 0.9, mpg = mpg + 2, state = 1)
states <- rbind(observed, changed)
moving <- ggplot(states, aes(wt, hp, z = mpg, group = id, colour = id)) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(PAL[c("blue", "orange", "teal")])) +
  coord_3d()

The tween specification inserts three frames between the two supplied states, producing five frames in total. Statistics run on the supplied states before interpolation, and all states train one set of scales.

movement <- animate_3d(moving, time = "state", tween = tween_3d(n = 3),
  renderer = "vector", width = 480, height = 360, fps = 5, progress = FALSE)
movement$frame_count
#> [1] 5
movement$transition
#>   from to fraction
#> 1    0  1     0.00
#> 2    0  1     0.25
#> 3    0  1     0.50
#> 4    0  1     0.75
#> 5    1  1     0.00

The first, middle and final frames show the three cars moving to their new positions. The camera and axis ranges remain fixed.

Group matching pairs occurrences within each persistent group. Map one identifier per moving mark when rows can change order. Source-row matching is also available, with row numbers interpreted within each state. Unmatched groups fade in or out by default; the enter and exit arguments can retain them or define starting and ending attributes.

Motion trails

The trail window counts preceding rendered frames, including the frames inserted by tween_3d(). Each moving mark leaves a tube whose alpha fades with age. A group identifier keeps each object’s history together when rows change order. Layers with fixed data appear in every frame, and gaps in an object’s observations break its trail.

wake <- animate_3d(moving, time = "state", tween = tween_3d(n = 3),
  trail = list(length = 4, radius = 0.05, taper = TRUE),
  renderer = "vector", width = 480, height = 360, progress = FALSE)

trail = 4 uses a default tube radius of 0.5% of the panel range diagonal. Setting width in the list selects a ribbon; normal sets its initial orientation. Radius and width use transformed position units. Mapped radius, width and twist aesthetics also reach the sweep. taper = TRUE multiplies the cross-section size by the age fraction used for fading. layers selects the indices of the moving layers that leave trails. Trails follow the frame-history approach of gganimate’s shadow_trail() and shadow_wake(), with connected surfaces built by the rotation-minimising tube and ribbon sweep.

Morph a surface

A surface with the same grid and mesh connectivity in every state can interpolate its heights and fill. Here the two states contain the same sampled wave with opposite signs. The middle frame is flat because every pair of heights averages to zero.

waves <- expand.grid(x = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 8),
                     y = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 8), state = 0:1)
waves$z <- with(waves, sin(pi * x) * cos(pi * y) * (1 - 2 * state))
wave <- ggplot(waves, aes(x, y, z = z, fill = z)) + geom_surface_3d() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = PAL["blue"], mid = "white", high = PAL["red"]) +
  coord_3d()
morph <- animate_3d(wave, time = "state", tween = tween_3d(n = 1),
  renderer = "vector", width = 480, height = 360, progress = FALSE)

Positions interpolate in transformed scale units, and colours interpolate in linear light. Paths with different vertex counts are resampled along their lengths. Polygon rings are aligned before interpolation. Meshes with changed connectivity cross-fade as complete shapes. See tween_3d() for matching and transition options.

Using gganimate

The state and time transitions of gganimate use a separate plot-building pipeline. Calling its animation renderer with those transitions and a 3D coordinate system produces guidance to use the native animation call. Build the ordinary 3D plot, supply its state column as the time argument, and add a tween specification, as in the examples above.

The native renderer evaluates visibility for each frame. Reuse of one geometry partition across successive camera frames is currently unavailable.

Explore the scene

The viewer opens one panel at its static camera position. Drag to orbit and use the wheel or a two-finger pinch to zoom. Arrow keys rotate the view; plus and minus change magnification.

if (requireNamespace("htmlwidgets", quietly = TRUE) &&
    requireNamespace("svglite", quietly = TRUE)) {
  view_3d(p, width = 560, height = 560)
}

Select Camera code to display the current coordinate call, then copy it into the plot code. Reset restores the initial camera. In a Shiny application, camera changes also update the input whose name is the widget identifier followed by _camera.

The viewer shows the whole plot: every facet panel is live, and the parts outside the panels (strips, legends, titles) are the static plot’s own, embedded as SVG around them. Orbiting one panel turns every panel by the same amount; view_3d(link = FALSE) moves each panel alone, and panel = shows one panel by itself.

Hovering a point, line, face or label shows its tooltip, and clicking selects it. Two aesthetics drive this, following ggiraph: tooltip sets the text, and data_id sets the selection key, so rows that share a key highlight together across layers. Without a tooltip, the tooltip lists the mapped values of the row. Shift-click adds a key to the selection, a click on empty space clears it, and unselected primitives dim while a selection exists. In Shiny, the input named by the widget identifier followed by _selected holds the selected keys.

cars <- data.frame(mtcars, model = rownames(mtcars))
picked <- ggplot(cars, aes(wt, mpg, z = hp, colour = factor(cyl),
    tooltip = model, data_id = model)) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 3) +
  coord_3d() +
  facet_wrap(~am)
if (requireNamespace("htmlwidgets", quietly = TRUE) &&
    requireNamespace("svglite", quietly = TRUE)) {
  view_3d(picked, width = 620, height = 360)
}

Linked brushing across widgets uses crosstalk: pass the SharedData whose origData() the plot draws as view_3d(plot, data = shared). Selections then travel between the viewer and the other widgets of the group, and a crosstalk filter hides the rows it removes.

The browser draws opaque geometry with a depth buffer, which records the nearest painted surface at each pixel. Transparent primitives are ordered by centre depth, so intersecting transparent surfaces can differ from static vector output. Browser labels use plain text. The pointer finds its primitive in an offscreen image of primitive identifiers, the same primitive_id the raster backend returns in its id buffer.

Camera conventions

The camera path keeps the plot data fixed. gganimate separates changes in data over time from its fixed view; the fixed-view principle informs the locked animation bounds here. rayshader’s movie renderer supplies the precedent for scalar and per-frame camera vectors and extension-selected encoders. rgl’s movie recorder and spin function supply the time-function pattern.

The viewer orbits around the coordinate system’s target and retains its projection and roll. Plotly’s scene camera exposes target, eye and up vectors with a projection choice. Dragging and wheel zoom follow three.js orbit controls. Geometry, colours and lighting travel to the browser once; camera changes are evaluated there.
